paras: The Warrenton manhunt for Andrew Jackson was an armed search by posses of more than 200 men for Andrew Jackson, alias Andrew Fields, a Black prisoner who escaped from the jail at Warrenton, Virginia, on August 9, 1920. The Washington Times reported open threats to lynch him, but he was back in jail within days and the town's mayor denied that any mob had threatened.

Jackson had been arrested about three weeks earlier, accused of attacking Mrs. J. B. Wilson, the wife of a prominent resident, who had raised him on her farm. She told police she was attacked while alone at home, and he was held for the grand jury.

On the afternoon of August 9, while jailor J. W. Shirley was closing the court house, Jackson climbed the stone wall around the jail. The search began with five men, but within an hour more than 200 men with rifles and revolvers, including prominent citizens, had joined it in three posses. He was surrounded on Mrs. George Smith's farm near Bealeton, where he had once lived with the Wilsons, but slipped away in the dark through tall corn.
According to the Warrenton dispatch, "open threats have been made," while influential residents urged the posses to turn him over to the authorities.
By August 14 Jackson, charged with attempted assault on a white woman, was again in the city jail; the coverage does not describe his recapture, and no report of a trial was found.

The Washington Times ran the escape on its front page as "Posses Hunt Negro Who Breaks Prison," with the deck "Pursuers Threaten Lynching Man Accused by Woman of Attacking Her." Five days later the Washington Herald answered with "Asserts Warrenton Lacks Mob Spirit," quoting Mayor Austin O. Weedon on the "peaceable and orderly manner" of the search. No Black-press coverage was found.
The Times' same-day dispatch reported open threats and a feared lynching; the mayor said afterward that there was no threat of a mob or riot and that intense feeling was absent.

accounts.label: Warrenton dispatch, Aug. 10
accounts.gist: More than 200 armed men hunted Jackson; feeling ran high, open threats were made and a lynching was feared if he was caught, though influential residents urged that he be handed to the authorities.

accounts.label: Mayor's statement
accounts.gist: Mayor Weedon said the search was peaceable and orderly, that intense feeling was absent, and that there was no threat of a mob or riot.

framing.detail: The Washington Times ran the escape on page one as 'POSSES HUNT NEGRO WHO BREAKS PRISON' with the deck 'Pursuers Threaten Lynching Man Accused by Woman of Attacking Her', calling him 'the negro' and treating the attack as alleged.
The Washington Herald printed the mayor's denial under 'ASSERTS WARRENTON LACKS MOB SPIRIT', presenting the town's view without comment.

versions.value: Feeling ran high, open threats were made, and a lynching was feared.
No threat of a mob or riot; intense feeling absent; search peaceable and orderly.

conflicts.note: The denial comes from the town's mayor after the recapture; the Times' report was a contemporaneous dispatch. Neither names who made threats.

versions.value: An attack on Mrs. J. B. Wilson.

conflicts.note: The Herald's later wording is the formal charge.

info: Jackson escaped from the Warrenton jail on the afternoon of Aug. 9, 1920, and the manhunt began within half an hour.
Warrenton, Va.; the trail led to Bealeton, where he was surrounded on the farm of Mrs. George Smith.
Andrew Jackson, alias Andrew Fields, a Black man ('negro', 'colored jail breaker'); not harmed in the reports.
Accused of attacking Mrs. J. B. Wilson, who had raised him on her farm; Herald gives the charge as attempted assault on a white woman.
Posses of armed residents, 'including some of the most prominent citizens' of the area.
